posts.quote: 41% Of Minneapolis 911 Staff Were Out. Walz's Paid Leave Lets New Hires Take It And Quit.
posts.alt: Photo of Minnesota Gov. Tim Walz in a blue suit and American flag lapel pin, speaking at an event in Glendale, Arizona, in August 2024. Text reads: 41% Of Minneapolis 911 Staff Were Out. Walz's Paid Leave Lets New Hires Take It And Quit. Break The Spin logo top left. Photo credit: Gage Skidmore, CC BY-SA 3.0.
posts.caption:
Governor Tim Walz signed it. He sold it as a win for working families. Eleven months later, Minneapolis 911 is paying the price.

At an October budget meeting, Emergency Communications Center Assistant Director Leticia Cardenas told the City Council that 41% of her 911 staff were out on Minnesota's new Paid Family and Medical Leave program.

The people left on the phones had to work overtime just to keep the center staffed around the clock. The 911 department went over budget in the second quarter "for the first time in a long time," Deputy City Controller Rob Lange said, because of overtime and paid leave.

The Minnesota Star Tribune reported that 854 Minneapolis city employees have used the program this year. The city has about 4,000 full-time workers. That's almost one in four.

Walz signed the law in May 2023. It took effect in January. Workers can take up to 12 weeks of family leave and up to 12 weeks of medical leave, capped at 20 weeks in a year, at partial pay, funded by a payroll tax. Employers still have to cover the empty chairs.

Councilmember Linea Palmisano asked Cardenas whether a new hire can take the paid leave right away, then quit when it ends.

"Yes to both of those," Cardenas said.

"Currently the way that the PFMLA is written up is that upon hire with the city, PFMLA can be utilized by any city employee. And then if they decided they wanted to quit working, they can choose to do that."

Walz is on his way out. He abandoned his reelection bid in January. The law stays. The 911 calls don't stop. And the people who sold this as compassion are not the ones working the extra shifts.
posts.first:
The facts: Tim Walz signed the law (H.F. 2, Laws 2023, Chapter 59) in May 2023. Benefits began Jan. 1, 2026. Workers can take up to 12 weeks of family leave and 12 weeks of medical leave per year, capped at 20 weeks if both are used, with partial pay funded by a payroll tax. Job protections generally begin 90 days after hire. Benefits also depend on a prior-year Minnesota earnings test (about $3,900 for 2026). City spokesperson Jess Olstad told the Star Tribune that 854 of about 4,000 Minneapolis full-time city employees have used the program in 2026, with 60 more under review. Cardenas told the City Council Budget Committee in early October that 41% of Emergency Communications Center staff were out on the program. The department proposed a $1.5 million budget increase, driven by salaries and overtime. Walz announced Jan. 5, 2026, that he would not seek a third term. Amy Klobuchar won the 2026 race to succeed him.

Sources: Minnesota Star Tribune (Nov. 23), Better Minneapolis (Oct. 7), Fox News (Nov. 25), Daily Wire (Nov. 24), Alpha News, official Minnesota Paid Leave guidance, Minnesota Senate DFL (May 25, 2023), Minnesota Laws 2023 Ch. 59 / LegiScan H.F. 2, MPR News (Jan. 5 and Nov. 3), AP.
